PullRequest.Title: Add ARM64 Linux Snap builds with selectable core22/core24 bases
PullRequest.Body:
Build ARM64 Linux Snap artifacts from native-architecture staged libraries, keeping core24 as the default and offering core22 for unpublished validation builds.

## Changes
- Use pinned amd64/arm64 Snapcraft 8 builders with matching Ubuntu package mirrors; reject mislabeled executable architectures before packing.
- Render base-specific Snapcraft architecture syntax, desktop libraries, and RPATH. The launcher reads the installed snap's base rather than hard-coding core20/core24.
- Wire the ARM64 product artifact and sanity target, add focused packaging tests, and document native install and release gates. Core26 can be packed locally on native Ubuntu 26.04 with Snapcraft 9+, but is not enabled in product CI without a verified multiarch builder.

## Related
Refs microsoft/vscode#125120 and microsoft/vscode#269552. Related to base/runtime report microsoft/vscode#241636. This is a follow-up/alternative to microsoft/vscode#298237 and microsoft/vscode#271464; please coordinate overlapping changes rather than merging both independently. It does not claim to fix their separate alternatives-registration or terminal-environment work. Do not close the ARM64 issues until snaps are available in the Store.

## Validation and remaining work
- `node --test build/lib/test/buildSnap.test.ts`: 34 passing on the current head commit.
- Shell syntax, patch whitespace, changed Azure YAML files, and six rendered base/architecture manifests validated; TypeScript editor diagnostics clear. The five initial hygiene errors and two Copilot review findings were addressed in ae3f27160f8, and the follow-up ESLint warning was fixed in f3985918b87. **Compile & Hygiene now passes** on the current head; other CI jobs may still be running.
- **Not yet verified:** an Azure product Snap build, native Ubuntu ARM64 install/desktop test, or Snap Store promotion. Before merge, run an unpublished product build (`VSCODE_PUBLISH=false`, `VSCODE_RUN_ARTIFACT_SANITY_TESTS=true`) and complete native ARM64 validation. The ARM64 artifact sanity job currently downloads the snap but cannot launch it on the x64 runner.

## Policy / maintainer coordination
The VS Code PR Check currently fails because a community-classified PR may not modify protected engineering files under `build/` or `build/azure-pipelines/`. The check requires a team-member-authored PR, a head commit signed by a trusted team-member key, or authorized automation; simply making this commit GitHub Verified would **not** satisfy it. Please have a VS Code build maintainer review and adopt/cherry-pick the relevant changes rather than bypassing the policy. This PR is for review and coordination, not an assertion that the release gate has passed.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The before/after grouping is explicit in one changed hunk, and the shared template proves every duplicated setup boundary. Only queue-time magnitude is uncertain; the repeated work is unconditional for the stated flags.
Findings.PerformanceResource: An additional CI agent plus duplicate checkout, Node/cache setup, sanity-test compilation, Key Vault access, and test-runner processes
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Every artifact-sanity run with both the default Linux and Snap targets enabled now starts a second x64 sanity job for one Snap test, duplicating fixed harness setup once per product build regardless of artifact size.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Lower CI throughput and additional agent/network load; under finite pool capacity the extra job also increases queueing and artifact-sanity completion latency.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The existing artifact_ubuntu_x64 job downloaded the x64 Snap alongside the other Linux artifacts and its linux(-deb|-snap)?-x64 grep ran the Snap test in the same initialized sanity harness.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The diff removes the Snap from that grouped job and adds a standalone artifact_ubuntu_snap_x64 sanity-tests.yml job, repeating all common job setup before running only linux-snap-x64.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The hunk changes the existing grep from linux(-deb|-snap)?-x64 to linux(-deb)?-x64, removes vscode_client_linux_x64_snap from its artifacts, and adds the separate artifact_ubuntu_snap_x64 job at line 1097 for that same Snap target.
Findings.Title: Keep the x64 Snap in the grouped Linux sanity job
Findings.Impact: Default artifact validation now allocates and initializes another Linux agent solely for a test that was already coalesced with the x64 Linux suite before this PR.
Findings.Evidence: common/sanity-tests.yml performs a sparse checkout, pipeline artifact download, Node installation, cache restore (and npm ci on a miss), sanity TypeScript compilation, Azure Key Vault retrieval, and a runner invocation per template instance. The new x64 instance duplicates those boundaries; warm caches avoid only npm ci, not checkout, compilation, Key Vault, or process startup. Jobs can run in parallel, so exact wall-clock impact is pool-dependent, but total work and agent demand always increase.
Findings.Recommendation: When VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX is true, keep the x64 Snap artifact and grep in artifact_ubuntu_x64 as before; instantiate the standalone Snap job only when the normal Linux target is disabled, matching the conditional coalescing already used by the non-artifact sanity section.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The trigger is explicit in the added condition, and the transitive template's unconditional build steps and outputs prove the extra work. Exact duration varies with caches and agent speed, but the full unrelated artifact cardinality is not uncertain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: ARM64 client/server build CPU, package filesystem operations, and pipeline-artifact upload bytes
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For every product run with VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_SNAP=true and VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_ARM64=false, the condition adds one complete ARM64 Linux product job; that job unconditionally produces and publishes the client archive, server, web server, DEB, and RPM in addition to the requested Snap.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Lower CI throughput and a longer Linux-stage critical path from building and uploading five unrelated ARM64 deliverables.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: With VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_ARM64=false, the ARM64 product job was not instantiated; enabling the x64 Snap did not cause ARM64 client/server/DEB/RPM work.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new OR condition instantiates the general-purpose Linux_arm64 job whenever Snap is enabled, even when the separate ARM64 product target is explicitly disabled.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The changed condition at line 483 adds eq(parameters.VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_SNAP, true) as an alternative to VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_ARM64. The selected linux/product-build-linux.yml template has unconditional outputs for the ARM64 archive, server, web server, DEB, and RPM, and its compile template unconditionally builds those packages before the conditional Snap step.
Findings.Title: Keep Snap-only builds from running every ARM64 target
Findings.Impact: A realistic Snap-only validation run that disables VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_ARM64 still consumes a full additional ARM64 product agent and waits for unrelated server and package work before the Snap artifact is available.
Findings.Evidence: Tracing the added branch into build/azure-pipelines/linux/product-build-linux.yml shows unconditional client/server/web/DEB/RPM artifact declarations, while product-build-linux-compile.yml builds DEB and RPM before the Snap block. Thus a Snap-only ARM64 request does not merely prepare the client needed by Snap; it executes and uploads all standard ARM64 targets. The duplicated condition in product-build-template.yml has the same behavior.
Findings.Recommendation: Pass a snap-only mode to the ARM64 job or create a dedicated ARM64 Snap job that builds the required client and Snap but skips server/web/DEB/RPM generation and outputs when VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_ARM64 is false.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The x64 host, QEMU registration, arm64 container platform, and full Snapcraft call path are explicit. The exact slowdown is agent-dependent, which limits severity, but the translated CPU mechanism and critical-path placement are certain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: CPU instructions and package/compression subprocess work executed through QEMU user-mode translation
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Every ARM64 Snap build runs the entire Snapcraft 8 container as linux/arm64 on the Linux stage's x64 host; the translated work includes Snapcraft, Apt/dpkg staging of all manifest packages, priming, and LZO package creation.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Higher ARM64 packaging latency and x64 agent CPU consumption, with the serial ARM64 Linux job delaying its artifact publication and downstream artifact sanity stage.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The pipeline built only the x64 Snap, natively in an x64 container; no ARM64 Snapcraft workload ran under CPU emulation.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The added step registers ARM64 QEMU emulation on the x64 Linux stage, after which build-snap.sh invokes the Snapcraft image with --platform linux/arm64 and performs the complete destructive pack inside it.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Line 419 newly registers qemu-user-static specifically for the ARM64 branch. The enclosing Linux stage is pinned to 1es-ubuntu-22.04-x64, and build-snap.sh's added pack_snap path runs docker --platform linux/$SNAP_ARCH ... snapcraft pack --destructive-mode for arm64.
Findings.Title: Pack ARM64 snaps on a native ARM64 worker
Findings.Impact: Each requested ARM64 Snap spends the complete pack phase under emulation; on product/release builds this can make the ARM64 job the slow tail and consumes materially more agent CPU than native execution.
Findings.Evidence: The call path is product-build.yml Linux stage (x64 pool) -> product-build-linux-compile.yml ARM64 branch -> QEMU registration -> build-snap.sh -> an arm64 Snapcraft container. resources/linux/snap/snapcraft.yaml stages the desktop dependency set and uses LZO compression, so emulation covers substantial package-processing work rather than a small architecture check. The repository already references the native 1es-azure-linux-3-arm64 pool for Linux ARM64 jobs, establishing a bounded native scheduling option.
Findings.Recommendation: Split ARM64 Snap preparation/packing into a job on the existing native ARM64 pool (or otherwise run the arm64 Snapcraft container on an ARM64 host), transferring only the prepared client input, while retaining the x64 job for cross-built non-Snap artifacts.

Scenarios.Scenario: Default product build with x64 and ARM64 core24 Snap artifacts enabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The x64 and ARM64 Linux jobs run in parallel, but each job serially prepares and packs its Snap before codesigning/moving outputs and publishing artifacts. Artifact sanity depends on completion of the Linux stage, so the slower ARM64 pack can gate validation and overall build completion.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Register qemu-user-static and run the linux/arm64 Snapcraft 8 container on an x64 host
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One QEMU registration and one successful full Snapcraft invocation per ARM64 Snap build; up to four serial invocations only for an early HTTP-429 before any parts run
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No ARM64 Snap was packed; the existing x64 Snap ran in an x64 builder without architecture emulation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The full translated Snapcraft/Apt/dpkg/prime/compression workload must finish before the ARM64 artifact can be moved and published

ExpensiveBoundaries.Location: build/azure-pipelines/linux/build-snap.sh and product-build-linux-compile.yml ARM64 Snap block
ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Pull pinned Snapcraft/QEMU images and retrieve staged Ubuntu packages
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Up to two Snapcraft image pulls and one QEMU image pull per build on cold Docker caches, plus package retrieval independently for x64 and ARM64
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Only the x64 internal Snapcraft image and x64 staged packages were required.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cold pulls and package downloads block each architecture's serial pack step

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Prepare the complete Snap source, stage/prime packages, create an LZO Snap, delete symlinks, and recursively make the source readable for SBOM
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One full source tree and one Snap per enabled architecture
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same broad flow existed for x64 only; the diff adds the ARM64 copy and its post-pack permission walk.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: All operations are in the package-build critical path; x64 and ARM64 are parallel but each tree is processed serially within its job

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish x64 and ARM64 Snap pipeline artifacts and generate SBOM from each prepared source
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One Snap artifact and one SBOM input tree per enabled architecture
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Only the x64 Snap artifact/SBOM boundary existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Artifact availability and downstream artifact sanity wait for publication

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One complete prepared VS Code tree and the Snap manifest's staged desktop-package set per architecture; ARM64 cost grows with files and packages processed by Snapcraft under emulation, not with a deduplicated group shared with x64.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One Linux job per architecture runs concurrently. Inside the ARM64 job, QEMU registration and Snapcraft packing are serial; retry attempts are also serial and occur only for the bounded pre-parts HTTP-429 case.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Docker image layers may be warm on a reused agent, but the script mounts no Apt/package cache, so staged package resolution and package processing occur for each job. Retry behavior is bounded to four attempts and refuses to retry after parts or a partial Snap exist.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the Linux stage's x64 pool, QEMU registration, linux/arm64 Docker platform, and full Snapcraft call path are all directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact QEMU slowdown, image-cache hit rate, and whether ARM64 becomes the longest parallel job vary by agent; the architecture translation over the complete pack path is explicit.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable: the ARM64 pack performs substantial package work under QEMU despite an existing native ARM64 pool, creating avoidable CPU and critical-path amplification.

Scenarios.Scenario: Snap-only product validation with VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_SNAP=true and VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_ARM64=false
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The added OR condition creates the general Linux_arm64 product job. That job must compile/package all of its unconditional client, server, web, DEB, and RPM outputs before and around the requested Snap step; Linux-stage completion and artifact validation wait for it.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run the general ARM64 Linux compile and client/server/web/DEB/RPM packaging pipeline
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One complete ARM64 product job per Snap-enabled run even when the ARM64 target is disabled; five non-Snap deliverable families are produced
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: With VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_ARM64=false no ARM64 Linux product job was instantiated.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The job must complete for the Linux stage and for downstream artifact sanity

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Upload unconditional ARM64 client, server, web, DEB, and RPM pipeline artifacts and associated SBOM data
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Five unrelated artifact families plus the requested Snap per affected run
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: None of these ARM64 outputs existed in this selector combination.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Uploads consume agent/network capacity before the job is complete and artifacts become available

Scenarios.ScalingInput: The complete ARM64 client/server/web trees and package payloads; work scales with all files and native modules in five non-Snap deliverables rather than only the client tree required for the Snap.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: A single ARM64 product job performs its build/package steps mostly serially, alongside the x64 job. The unrelated ARM64 outputs are not coalesced away based on the disabled ARM64 selector.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Node-module caches can reduce dependency installation, but compilation, server/web assembly, DEB/RPM packaging, SBOM traversal, and artifact publication still occur. There is no negative/selection cache that suppresses outputs when VSCODE_BUILD_LINUX_ARM64 is false.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed selector and all transitive unconditional build/output declarations are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The saved time from a snap-only mode depends on cache state and which compile step dominates, but the unrelated packages and uploads are unconditional.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable: a selector intended to request Snap packaging now eagerly expands a disabled ARM64 target into a full product build instead of a bounded Snap-only path.

Scenarios.Scenario: Artifact sanity validation when normal Linux and Snap targets are both enabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: ArtifactSanityTestsLinux waits for the Linux stage, then launches the general x64 Linux job, a new standalone x64 Snap job, and a new ARM64 download-only job. Jobs can run in parallel, but stage completion waits for all and finite pool capacity can queue them.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Sparse checkout, Cache service access, Azure Key Vault secret retrieval, and pipeline-artifact download for the standalone x64 Snap job
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One additional set of fixed network boundaries per artifact-sanity run; artifact bytes are one Snap and were previously downloaded by the grouped job
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The x64 Snap artifact was downloaded and tested inside the existing artifact_ubuntu_x64 job.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs in parallel when agents are available, but consumes another agent and can extend stage completion through queueing or its own setup latency

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Install/select Node, optionally npm ci, compile sanity tests, and invoke the Ubuntu sanity runner
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One duplicated harness compilation and runner process tree for one x64 Snap test per run
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: One initialized x64 harness ran archive, DEB, and Snap tests together.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The standalone job must complete before the artifact sanity stage completes

ExpensiveBoundaries.Location: build/azure-pipelines/product-build.yml ARM64 Snap artifact job and test/sanity/src/desktop.test.ts
ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Download the ARM64 Snap artifact in a download-only sanity job
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One ARM64 Snap artifact download and one full harness initialization per enabled artifact-sanity run
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No ARM64 Snap artifact or validation job existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: No ARM64 executable runs; the download-only job still participates in stage completion

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Fixed setup once per job plus downloaded artifact bytes. The regression is one extra complete x64 harness setup per artifact-sanity run, independent of the single Snap test's size.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Up to three Linux sanity jobs run concurrently for x64 Linux, x64 Snap, and ARM64 Snap download. Each template instance independently initializes its harness; no shared sequencer or setup coalescing exists across jobs.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The sanity node_modules cache is keyed consistently and can be warm, avoiding npm ci. Even warm, each job performs checkout, Node task setup, cache service access, TypeScript compilation, Key Vault access, and runner startup; simultaneous cold jobs may not coalesce cache population.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the old grouped grep/artifact and new standalone template invocation are in the same changed hunk, and the common template enumerates every repeated boundary.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Parallel execution may hide some x64 wall-clock cost when agents are immediately available; total CPU/network work and agent demand always increase, and queue impact depends on pool load.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable for the x64 split: it duplicates a complete harness job for a test that was already coalesced. The new ARM64 download boundary is required by the feature and was not separately reported.

Scenarios.Scenario: Launching an installed VS Code Snap after install/update and on warm repeated launches
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The launcher synchronously normalizes SNAP, reads meta/snap.yaml with awk, validates the base, initializes environment state, waits for update-time asynchronous cache builders, then execs Electron. On warm launches only the metadata read and normal launcher setup remain.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read installed meta/snap.yaml and parse its base with awk
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One small file read and one awk process per Snap launch
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The launcher used hard-coded core20 paths and did not read Snap metadata.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Synchronous before Electron exec, but bounded to a tiny fixed metadata file

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Compile gio modules, schemas, pixbuf loaders, and input modules after a Snap revision change
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most once per cache type per installed revision, with concurrent execution followed by a wait
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same update-time cache builders existed with hard-coded core20 tool paths; the diff only selects the installed base.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: First launch after update waits; warm launches skip the work

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One small installed metadata file per process launch; no collection or history growth. Update-time work scales with existing schema/module files and remains once per Snap revision.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: On first launch after a revision, gio modules, schemas, pixbuf loaders, and input modules can run concurrently through async_exec but the launcher waits for all before exec. Warm launches skip those update tasks. The new base read is one synchronous subprocess per launch.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: SNAP_DESKTOP_LAST_REVISION is the positive warm-state marker. A changed revision triggers cache rebuild and then records the revision; normal repeated launches are warm. Base metadata is not cached and is reread each launch.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for one synchronous read/process per launch; low magnitude and bounded scale make it non-reportable.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The fixed awk startup cost varies by machine and Snap confinement, but there is no realistic cardinality or lifetime growth.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: the metadata lookup is fixed-size one-per-launch work and does not meet the bar for a concrete performance regression; changed base paths do not increase update-time cache-builder cardinality.

Scenarios.Scenario: Preparing Snap manifests and running the new focused packaging tests
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Gulp renders one manifest per requested architecture/base before packing. The focused Node test suite creates isolated temporary trees and synchronous mock subprocesses only when explicitly run in build validation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read templates, copy the prepared application tree, and write the rendered snapcraft manifest
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same prepare-snap task copied/rendered an x64 source; the diff adds bounded token replacements and ARM64 invocation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Spawn mocked build/launcher shell scripts in focused tests
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Bounded by the explicit packaging test matrix when that test file is run
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The focused packaging test file did not exist.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Only affects test execution, not product build unless the focused suite is selected

Scenarios.ScalingInput: A fixed set of template tokens and, in tests, the six base/architecture combinations plus bounded negative cases.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Manifest replacement is a single local stream; tests run according to node:test scheduling but each fixture owns a separate temporary root. No product-runtime concurrency is changed.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No persistent cache is introduced; temporary test trees are removed after each test. Product manifest rendering is repeated once per architecture as required.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: all loops and fixture lifecycles are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Test duration is not measured, but cardinality is small and bounded.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: added rendering and tests are bounded validation work with no hot-path or unbounded resource mechanism.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 22 changed files and every diff page. Reported three introduced CI performance regressions: full unrelated ARM64 product work in Snap-only selections, complete ARM64 Snapcraft packing under QEMU on an x64 stage, and loss of x64 artifact-sanity setup coalescing. Checked launcher startup, packaging retries/caches, SBOM preparation, artifact boundaries, and test fixture lifecycles; no additional high-confidence scaling or retention issue met the reporting bar.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
